#9717. Hindsight-Driven Development: An Iterative Approach to Building Software With AI

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI makes trying cheaper than guessing, yet spec-driven development still asks you to guess first. Meet Hindsight-Driven Development.

You spend two hours writing a detailed spec for a feature. An AI coding agent builds it in ten minutes. You try it, and within a minute you see what the spec got wrong.

In those same two hours, you could have built it, tried it, thrown away three versions, and kept the fourth.

Specs force us to make our most detailed decisions at the moment we know the least.

For decades, that was a fair trade. Building was expensive, so we paid to describe software first.

AI broke that trade. Yet a popular response to AI coding agents is spec-driven development. Tools like GitHub’s Spec Kit and Amazon’s Kiro have you write and sign off on requirements, a design, and a task list before the agent writes any code. More detail, decided earlier. That gets it backward.

Writing detailed specs for AI agents is waterfall, rebranded for the AI era.

Even when that spec gets edited later, you still decide before you see.

One exception, which I’ll come back to: decide up front whatever is expensive to undo. Build everything else.

Writing a spec means imagining a product that doesn’t exist yet and simulating it all in your head. That takes three kinds of guessing:

No amount of good writing fixes this. Imagination has limits. People don’t know what they want until they see what they don’t want. Yet the spec gets reviewed, approved, and signed off, and the guess gains an authority it never earned.

A spec can be perfectly clear, perfectly consistent, and completely wrong.

If you’ve ever shipped a feature exactly as specified and watched people ignore it, you already know the problem.

We get very good at building what we imagined, and never find out what we actually needed.

Agile admitted part of this problem. But building was still expensive. Three versions of one feature, just to see which felt right? Rarely worth the cost.

So the spec survived as user stories, tickets, and acceptance criteria. Agile shortened the distance between guessing and feedback. You still had to guess first.

Say you’re building a customer-support assistant. Should it ask two questions or five? Suggest a fix early, or wait? Will it feel helpful or pushy? Skip the meeting. Generate one and talk to it.

The first version asks too many questions, forgets what you told it, and jumps to answers too early. You see all three in minutes, and they produce better requirements than anything you’d write in advance.

You might say AI can write the spec in ten minutes too. It can, but only what you already imagine, and the limit was never typing. A faster spec is still a guess.

I call this Hindsight-Driven Development. A spec asks you to decide with foresight, before anything exists. This approach lets you decide with hindsight, after you’ve seen the real thing.

Start with one sentence of intent. Build a rough version, use it, and keep correcting it until it does what you want. The fastest hindsight comes from a real user, so put the rough version in front of one early. The corrections sound like this:

“This workflow is confusing.” “Don’t offer a refund before I’ve finished explaining.” “Show me three different approaches.”

Nobody writes “don’t offer a refund before I’ve finished explaining” into a spec. Everyone says it the first time the bot does it.

The third one matters most: asking for several approaches early stops you from polishing only the first idea.

Predicting what’s right is hard. Recognizing what’s wrong is easy. This approach trades the hard problem for the easy one.

Agile still writes each ticket first. Here, the product writes the next one.

And vibe coding accepts whatever the AI produces and moves on. Hindsight-Driven Development questions every result, corrects it, and keeps every correction as a test or a line in the spec.

Fred Brooks wrote “plan to throw one away” in 1975, then later called that too simple. His better lesson, from 1986: “grow, not build, software.”

Slack began as the in-house chat tool of a team building an online game. The game failed. The tool became the product. The idea is old. What changed is the price.

A prototype used to be a project. Now it’s a prompt.

They do. But a spec written in advance can’t cover a gap nobody knew was there.

Agents drift less from forgetting than from decisions we haven’t made yet.

When the agent guesses wrong, you see it the first time you use the product, and the fix costs minutes. That fix then goes into the tests, and the spec the agent reads next time.

What’s harmful is the spec written first, from foresight, by people asked to imagine what they can’t yet see. Hindsight-Driven Development flips the order: the spec comes last, from what the team has already seen.

Each person corrects the product from their own angle. Only the version you keep goes through code review, and the decisions behind it go into the spec. The ones you throw away cost a few minutes and nothing else.

Every checkable correction becomes an automated test, like “it should remember my order number.” A correction like “this feels confusing” stays a note in the spec until someone decides what better looks like. AI merges it all into one readable spec, flags where people disagree, and asks the team to settle it.

Nobody writes the spec. Everyone shapes it, and AI keeps it whole.

The testable parts stay matched to the product, because a test fails the moment they drift apart. The team aligns around the spec, and the agents read it too, so they stop guessing.

Spec-driven development with extra steps? The document may look the same, but here it records what people saw, not what they imagined.

And the risks no demo reveals, like security holes or failure under heavy load? You don’t guess those either. You inherit the rules others learned the hard way, and test for them. For everything else, workflows, features, and behavior nobody predicted, you discover it by building.

The exception I promised at the start: anything other people build on, like an API another team uses, a customer contract, or anything a regulator requires, is expensive to undo, so agree it up front. That list is short. Most of what a product does sits outside it.

AI now handles much of the slow part: writing the code. The bottleneck becomes deciding what to build, and that’s a job for the whole team: product, engineering, and architecture.

Even architecture works this way. A good design is never written in one go. It starts rough and gets refined, round after round. Until now, all that refining happened on paper. Now the architect refines the working product itself.

The scarce skill now is knowing what’s wrong when you see it.

We spent fifty years getting better at describing software before building it. That made sense when every line took real effort.

That’s no longer true. When a working version of a feature costs minutes, a detailed spec written before a single experiment is premature commitment dressed up as diligence.

For decades, we built with foresight. Now we can build with hindsight.

What’s the biggest thing your spec got wrong that you only saw once the product ran? Tell me in the responses. And if you think I’m wrong, tell me why.

#9715. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

#9714. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9713. From API to Decision-Ready Meteograms: Unlocking Global 15-Day Hourly Weather Forecasts with Python

In consumer weather apps, a brief summary like "light rain over the next three days, temperatures between 12°C and 18°C" compresses highly complex atmospheric physics into a single sentence. While sufficient for a daily commute, such coarse daily overviews fall short in rigorous data analysis and engineering applications. Whether you are forecasting solar photovoltaic (PV) power output at noon tomorrow, evaluating sudden wind gusts along an autonomous drone inspection route, or analyzing the exact onset and cessation of a precipitation event alongside shifting wind fields and cloud cover, you need continuously sampled hourly meteorological time-series data.

In this technical walkthrough, we explore the Global City Forecast API from Global Weather Data. Beyond demonstrating how to query the API in Python, we will focus on using Matplotlib to organize up to 23 meteorological variables into a clean, reproducible multi-panel meteogram—while systematically avoiding common engineering pitfalls such as timezone mismatches, mixed physical units, improper missing-value handling, and toponymic ambiguity.

Before writing any code, let's examine the data architecture provided by Global Weather Data. The platform organizes global meteorological resources into three core product lines, available both via RESTful APIs for automated data pipelines and as downloadable flat or multidimensional files:

These three products correspond to three distinct analytical perspectives in operational workflows:

Regarding delivery formats, CSV files integrate seamlessly into spreadsheet tools and standard tabular data workflows. Gridded datasets are delivered in NetCDF (Network Common Data Form), the industry-standard self-describing multidimensional array format in atmospheric and oceanic sciences, which pairs naturally with Python's xarray library for spatiotemporal slicing and scientific computing.

As noted in the product table above, forecast data is updated four times daily on a rolling basis. This schedule aligns with the four standard forecast cycles (or model runs) initiated daily at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) by major global Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models, such as ECMWF and GFS.

Consequently, a 15-day forecast for a given location is not a static table. Every few hours, as the latest global observations from meteorological satellites, weather radars, and surface stations undergo data assimilation (the process of fusing multi-source observations into an NWP model's initial state to minimize initial condition errors), a new model run computes an updated forecast trajectory. In production data engineering, we strongly recommend logging data provenance metadata—such as the request timestamp, query parameters, and API version—whenever persisting forecast data to disk. Without this metadata, conducting accurate model backtesting or post-event error analysis becomes nearly impossible, as you cannot verify which forecast cycle generated a given prediction.

Additionally, note that API rate limits and quotas vary by account tier; always review the official documentation before deploying batch ingestion scripts (basic accounts typically include up to 1,000 free API calls). Keep in mind that both city-level and gridded forecasts represent mesoscale background atmospheric conditions (spanning a few kilometers to several hundred kilometers horizontally) rather than street-level microclimates. Local topography, urban canopies, and the urban canyon effect in high-density built environments can all introduce noticeable deviations between localized in-situ measurements and grid-cell values.

Defining Operational Boundaries: A 15-day forecast is a numerical estimate of medium-range atmospheric evolution. Due to the nonlinear, chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics, forecast uncertainty grows with lead time, and medium-range forecasts must not be conflated with long-term climate projections. For safety-critical applications—such as aviation, maritime navigation, severe weather mitigation, or industrial safety—never rely solely on a single API chart. Always cross-reference official meteorological warnings, in-situ sensor observations, and industry safety protocols.

The Global City Forecast API uses a straightforward RESTful URL structure with path parameters:

Each request requires two core path parameters:

Among the three location formats, GeoNames ID (e.g., 5368361 for Los Angeles) is the most reliable choice for automated data pipelines. First, countless cities share identical names worldwide (there are dozens of settlements named Paris or Springfield), and a globally unique numeric ID eliminates toponymic ambiguity entirely. Second, city names containing spaces or special characters (like Los Angeles) require URL percent-encoding, whereas numeric IDs keep request URLs clean and predictable. If you pass coordinate pairs, ensure that the comma separating longitude and latitude is preserved unescaped during URL encoding.

Developers new to meteorological APIs often notice that the JSON payload is not structured as a conventional row-oriented list (i.e., an array of 361 objects, each containing all 23 keys for a single hour). Instead, the response uses the following structure:

This payload design reflects several deliberate engineering choices:

Our test query for Los Angeles returns 23 meteorological variables. The table below groups them by physical category (note that available fields may vary across product tiers; always rely on the keys returned in your live response):

To extract maximum operational value from these parameters, let's examine how meteorologists and domain engineers interpret key variable combinations:

Plotting 23 variables with vastly different physical units and magnitudes on a single vertical axis is impractical—atmospheric pressure (~10³ hPa) would flatten cloud cover (0--1) into an unreadable line along the bottom axis. The standard scientific visualization approach is to group variables by physical dimension and stack them vertically in a shared-time-axis multi-panel figure (sharex=True).

The complete Python script below is ready to run out of the box and incorporates several production-grade engineering practices:

First, install the required dependencies in your Python environment:

Save the following script as plot_weather_forecast.py. Replace API_KEY at the top with your personal credential, and modify LOCATION if you wish to query a different city. Running the script generates both a high-resolution PNG and a vector PDF in the same directory:

Several subtle design choices in the script above address common meteorological plotting challenges:

If your workflow requires exporting the forecast to a tabular file or feeding features into a machine learning model, the API's columnar JSON structure lets you build a DataFrame and compute resultant wind speeds in just a few vectorized lines:

Using np.hypot(u, v) computes the Euclidean norm sqrt(u² + v²) with C-level vectorization while guarding against numerical overflow, processing hundreds of hourly records instantaneously.

Once the multi-panel meteogram is generated, you can diagnose weather systems by scanning vertically across the shared timeline:

Combining 15-day medium-range visibility with hourly temporal resolution and global point coverage unlocks practical applications across numerous industries. In production systems, meteorological data serves as the primary environmental input, which must then be combined with domain-specific constraints and risk thresholds:

Finally, bear in mind a fundamental scientific distinction: do not conflate weather forecasting with climate change assessment. A 15-day hourly forecast addresses short- to medium-range atmospheric evolution. If your objective is to evaluate multi-decade drought trends, extreme heatwave frequency, or long-term wind resource bankability, do not extrapolate a 15-day forecast—instead, switch to the platform's Global City Historical Weather dataset (10+ years of hourly records) or dedicated climate reanalysis archives.

By exposing clean RESTful APIs and standard scientific file formats, Global Weather Data spares engineering teams the heavy lifting of ingesting and decoding raw meteorological bulletins (such as multi-gigabyte GRIB2 files from national weather centers). Once the data is in hand, what elevates a chart from a casual plot to a decision-ready engineering artifact is not merely a polished color palette—it is an unambiguous UTC time baseline, physically consistent unit groupings, explicit NaN handling for missing data, and clear provenance markers.

We hope this guide and the accompanying Python script serve as a practical addition to your meteorological data toolkit. Pick a target city, run the script, and start exploring how the atmosphere will evolve over the next fifteen days.

#9712. Four Relationships, One Second Brain: What You Need to Know

Building shared memory for AI agents. Writing Super Second Brain on memory, identity, and human agency.

Building shared memory for AI agents. Writing Super Second Brain on memory, identity, and human agency.

Building shared memory for AI agents. Writing Super Second Brain on memory, identity, and human agency.

Once fidelity becomes high enough, one day you hear something like this.

“On this issue, I think I know you better than you know yourself.”

People do not respond to those words in the same way. Some laugh, some take offense, and some hurt for a long time.

I read that difference along two axes I have used in earlier whitepapers.

The two axes are independent. Some people can bear reality without seeing it well; others see it well but struggle to bear it. That gives us four rooms.

Of the four rooms, ④ looks the most peaceful from the outside. The owner is satisfied, the AI complies, and there is no conflict. The second brain tells its owner what they want to hear with increasing sophistication. The uncomfortable things other people used to say are filtered out by the agent before they arrive.

Room ③ is noisy, but it moves. Pain means something is being seen, and someone who sees can make changes. As experiences of being wrong without falling apart accumulate, ③ moves toward ①.

Room ② is comfortable, and that is where it stops. In terms of the steps in Chapter 4, it has skipped the mirror and gone straight to the representative. The work runs well. But the person that the second brain comes to resemble is less the actual owner than the owner as described by the owner.

I do not want this table used to label people. The same person may be in ① at work and ③ with family. After a week without enough sleep, anyone can slide toward ④. I do, too.

The four rooms do not classify kinds of people. They are a hypothesis about the relationship someone has with a second brain in a particular domain and state. As in my earlier whitepapers, the principle is to look for recurring patterns rather than judge from a single scene.

The same second brain becomes another self for one person, an assistant for another, a mirror for another, and a mechanism for automating self-deception for another.

The two table images reproduce the existing English translation of the author’s original tables. The Korean originals are included in the review package. This essay is part of the ongoing Super Second Brain whitepaper.

If AI Shares Your Memories and Values, Are You Still the Original?

#9710. pandas merge() Returned More Rows Than You Started With? Catch Duplicate Keys with validate=

You left-joined 4 orders onto a customer table and got back 6 rows. Worse, the revenue column went from 520 to 830, and nobody noticed until the report reached a manager.

merge() did exactly what it was told. A left join keeps every left row, but if a key appears twice on the right, every matching left row is copied once per match. No error, no warning, just quietly inflated numbers.

Here is how to reproduce it, catch it automatically, and fix the three key problems that cause most "wrong row count" merges.

Customer 10 has two rows (an old address and a new one), so orders 1 and 4 each come back twice:

Before blaming the join, look at the lookup table:

keep=False marks every copy, so you see all the conflicting rows side by side and can decide which one is correct.

This is the part most tutorials skip. merge() has a validate= argument that checks the relationship you expect and raises if the data disagrees:

The options are "one_to_one", "one_to_many", "many_to_one" and "many_to_many" (which checks nothing). Many orders per customer, one row per customer, is many_to_one. Put this on every merge in a pipeline that feeds a report: it turns a silent wrong number into a loud failure on the day the lookup table changes.

Calling drop_duplicates() on the result hides the problem and can drop legitimate rows. Decide which lookup row wins, dedupe the right side, then merge with the check still on:

If you have an updated_at column, sort by it first so keep="last" really means "most recent", rather than "whatever order the CSV happened to be in".

Sometimes the count is right but half the joined columns are NaN. Add indicator=True to see which rows actually matched:

left_only rows found no partner. Here it is a trailing space in "B2 " and lowercase "c3". Normalize both sides before joining:

Mismatched key types. If one side read IDs as numbers and the other as strings (common after read_excel or a JSON API), pandas 3.0 stops you:

Convert explicitly with .astype(...) on one side. Don't just cast both to str, or 10 and "10.0" will never match.

NaN keys match each other. Unlike SQL, pandas treats missing keys as equal:

One missing key on the left just turned into two joined rows. Drop or fill null keys (df.dropna(subset=["k"])) before merging unless you really want them paired.

If you want a refresher on how inner, left, right and outer joins differ (with diagrams and row counts for each), I wrote it up in pandas merge: inner, left, right and outer join examples. When your data starts life in spreadsheets, reading and writing Excel files with openpyxl covers the import side. And if a key column comes from an API, the free JSON formatter on Blogs World makes it easy to spot a stray string ID or trailing space before it reaches your join.

#9707. Three Correlations Passed Validation. The Matrix Was Impossible.

A risk dashboard can look completely convincing while displaying numbers from a model that should never have accepted its inputs.

Imagine a UI with three correlation sliders:

And yet no three random variables can have all three of those pairwise correlations at once.

This isn't a report of a production failure. It's a failure mode we explicitly designed against while building a browser-based portfolio-risk visualization. The surprising part is that the bug can live entirely in the inputs, before any rendering code runs. The matrix that looks valid Our three sliders produce:

A [ 1.00, 0.90, 0.90 ] B [ 0.90, 1.00, -0.90 ] C [ 0.90, -0.90, 1.00 ]

The following check is necessary, but insufficient:

It returns true. That proves only that individual cells are in range.

A correlation matrix has to describe a jointly possible system. Its entries are constrained by one another.

There is a geometric intuition: if B closely follows A, and C also closely follows A, then B and C cannot simultaneously behave as almost exact opposites. The three statements conflict. Why the determinant exposes the contradiction For a symmetric three-asset correlation matrix with off-diagonal entries a, b, and c, its determinant is:

In this example, a = 0.9, b = 0.9, and c = -0.9, so:

det(R) = 1 + 2(0.9)(0.9)(-0.9) - 3(0.9²) = -2.888

A real correlation matrix must be positive semidefinite (PSD): for every vector x, the quadratic form xᵀRx must be nonnegative. That is what makes it possible to interpret the matrix as correlations coming from a covariance matrix.

This particular matrix has eigenvalues -0.8, 1.9, and 1.9. A negative eigenvalue is enough to show it is not PSD.

Here's another way to see it. Take x = [-1, 1, 1]. Then xᵀRx = -2.4. If R were a covariance matrix of unit-variance variables, that would claim a linear combination has negative variance. That's impossible.

One nuance: a bad correlation matrix does not necessarily produce a negative variance for every long-only portfolio. It is invalid globally, even if one portfolio happens to produce a nonnegative result. That's why validating only the final variance is not enough.

You can also derive the allowable third correlation when the first two are fixed:

For a = b = 0.9, the range is 0.62 ≤ c ≤ 1.00. A value of -0.9 is nowhere near feasible.

Changing c to +0.8 creates a valid matrix with determinant +0.036. But an application should not silently change a user's assumption. Fixing or projecting a matrix is a modeling choice that deserves an explanation. A tiny JavaScript engine you can run The example below deliberately has three assets so the PSD test fits in one formula. It is a self-contained teaching implementation, not a copy of our production module and not a generic validator for matrices of any size.

It also demonstrates a second engineering invariant: the sum of Euler volatility contributions must equal portfolio volatility whenever that quantity is defined.

Run it with Node.js (tested with Node 22.16.0):

Nothing here calls an API or downloads price data. The weights, volatilities, and correlations are hypothetical decimals, not historical estimates or investment recommendations. The important part is what we test For risk software, a nice-looking result isn't an acceptance test. We want a handful of invariants that can fail loudly:

Result: six tests pass on the code above. The valid example uses weights 40% / 35% / 25%, individual annualized volatilities 30% / 20% / 15%, and pairwise correlations 0.9 / 0.9 / 0.8. It calculates 21.938% modeled portfolio volatility. Its contributions are 11.856, 6.637, and 3.444 volatility percentage points—not three independent asset volatilities.

The units matter: 0.20 means 20% annualized volatility; 0.20 is not 0.20 percentage points. Errors here can be just as misleading as a bad matrix. This is a UI architecture problem, too In MarketDeck's Risk Constellation, the live public educational lab models four fictional assets. It calculates covariance, portfolio volatility, and Euler risk contributions in a numerical engine rather than inferring them from how far a line stretches on screen. Its public equal-correlation slider is constrained to a safe 0...1 range; you cannot paste the impossible three-asset matrix into that public UI.

The engineering lesson is still useful for any application that accepts independently edited pairwise assumptions:

It's a small experiment, but it carries a general engineering lesson: A set of individually plausible inputs is not necessarily a mathematically possible system.

That's true in finance, numerical simulation, ML feature engineering, and many applications where relationships are entered pair by pair.

References: Higham, Computing the Nearest Correlation Matrix, Node.js built-in test runner.

Disclosure: This article and its illustrative code were drafted with substantial AI assistance. The mathematical definitions were checked against the MarketDeck model and numerical references, and the included JavaScript example was executed with six passing tests. A human publisher should review the final text before releasing it. The example is educational only.

#9706. Your Context Is the New Moat: Here's Why

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Jack Dorsey says there is no moat anymore. Yet, Palantir is up 668% in five years, Instinct is valued at $10 billion, and Emergent hit $100 million in annualized revenue in eight months. Both can’t be true unless the moat moved.

My bet: it moved to context. The software that wins from here will behave less like a tool and more like a consultant who knows your business deeply: one that tells you what to do, and then does much of it for you.

The cost of building software is collapsing, and agents can now do real work, so everyone is asking. Jack Dorsey (co-founder of Twitter and Square) says there is none; others say distribution is the moat, and Karri Saarinen (Linear CEO) argues that individual taste will always create moats.

https://x.com/jack/status/2114121702515114234

None of them won on the ability to build software. Technically, anyone can release an assistant; Instinct is still worth $10 billion. They won on knowing the customer’s world well enough to do the work, not just support it.

Palantir, built on embedding deeply in how each customer operates, is the clearest case:

The old moats were the ability to build software, owning the customer, and feature breadth with its integrations and switching costs. Now that software can be generated, the first and the last no longer count. The new moats are:

The difference matters. Code can be generated in an afternoon. Context can’t: it builds up from use, decisions, and outcomes, and it compounds.

You can already see the shift. Google Ads’ auto-applied recommendations adjust your campaigns based on your own account’s history, and Shopify Sidekick answers questions and takes actions using your store’s data.

If context is the moat, the practical question is where it lives. The agent world has quietly settled on an almost embarrassingly simple answer: plain Markdown files the agent reads before it acts. That’s the harness: the files, triggers, and tools around a model that decide what it knows and when it moves.

Look at OpenClaw, an open-source personal agent, or gstack, Garry Tan’s open-source Claude Code setup. Each file answers one question:

A chat, a schedule, or an event triggers the agent. It reads those files, then understands, acts, and checks, using tools like a browser, APIs, and code. The result is an answer or completed work.

For an online store, the harness comes down to five files. What makes them work is being specific. Here’s what they might say for a skincare brand:

Now put a harness like this inside a real store. On day one, it simply sets honest expectations: Sam’s first sale will usually take six to seven days.

By month two, it doesn’t wait to be asked. Sam’s Goals.md says returns should be under 4% by December; they’re at 5.8%. So it brings three questions worth asking, each with a “Research this” button.

And when there’s work to do, it says so: nine listings with reduced visibility, fourteen photos to fix, three listings flagged in reviews. Next to each one is a single button: Do it for me.

Start with the five files. Write down your goals, your principles, how your KPIs actually break down, the patterns you’ve already learned, and your users. Write them in plain Markdown, and keep them current.

That’s what turns software from a tool that runs a workflow into something closer to a high-powered consultant with very deep insight into your business: one that tells you what you should be doing, and then does a lot of it on your behalf.

#9705. How TLS Protects Your Internet Connection: The Complete Guide

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at cryptkit.dev • AI-assisted

Every time you visit a website, send an API request, or receive a message, TLS (Transport Layer Security) is working silently in the background. The padlock icon in your browser's address bar is its visible signal — but the cryptography behind it involves a sophisticated combination of every primitive we've covered across this blog.

TLS is not a single algorithm. It is a protocol orchestration that combines symmetric encryption, asymmetric key exchange, digital signatures, hash functions, and message authentication into a single handshake that completes in milliseconds. Understanding how TLS works means understanding how all these pieces fit together — and why each one is indispensable.

This guide walks through the TLS 1.3 handshake step by step, maps each phase to the cryptographic primitive it relies on, compares TLS 1.2 and 1.3, and gives you practical configuration guidance.

A Brief History: From SSL to TLS 1.3 Year Version Key Milestone 1994 SSL 1.0 Netscape's first attempt (never publicly released) 1995 SSL 2.0 First public release; quickly found to have serious flaws 1996 SSL 3.0 Complete redesign; basis for all TLS versions 1999 TLS 1.0 IETF takes over; essentially SSL 3.1 2006 TLS 1.1 Added protection against CBC attacks 2008 TLS 1.2 SHA-2 cipher suites, AEAD modes, customizable PRFs 2018 TLS 1.3 1-RTT handshake, mandatory forward secrecy, removed all legacy algorithms TLS 1.0 and 1.1 were deprecated by RFC 8996 in March 2021. TLS 1.2 remains widely used and is still considered secure when properly configured. TLS 1.3 is the current gold standard, supported by all major browsers and servers since 2018–2020.

The TLS Handshake: Phase by Phase The TLS handshake is the process where two parties (typically a browser and a server) establish a secure connection. Think of it as a negotiation: "Here's what I can do" → "Here's what I think is best" → "Here's proof I am who I say I am" → "Let's start encrypting."

Phase 1: Client Hello (The Opening Bid) The client initiates the connection by sending:

Protocol version — disguised as TLS 1.2 (0x0303) for middlebox compatibility, with the real version (TLS 1.3 = 0x0304) in the supported_versions extension 32 bytes of random data — the ClientRandom, used later in key derivation Cipher suite list — in TLS 1.3, only three AEAD suites are defined: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 Supported groups — elliptic curves for key exchange: X25519, P-256, P-384, P-521, X448, ffdhe2048–8192 Signature algorithms — ECDSA-P256-SHA256, Ed25519, RSA-PSS-SHA256, etc. Key share — the client's ephemeral public key (e.g., an X25519 public key, 32 bytes) SNI (Server Name Indication) — the hostname the client wants to reach Crypto primitives involved: Random number generation for ClientRandom, elliptic curve math for the key share.

Phase 2: Server Hello (The Response) The server replies with:

Selected cipher suite — one from the client's list (e.g., TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384) 32 bytes of ServerRandom Key share — the server's ephemeral public key (same curve as the client's) Supported version — confirms TLS 1.3 At this point, both sides have each other's ephemeral public keys. They can now compute a shared secret using elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH).

Phase 3: Key Derivation (The Mathematical Magic) This is where the real cryptography happens. Both client and server independently compute the same set of session keys — without ever transmitting them.

Each side multiplies the other's public key by their own private key on the agreed elliptic curve. Due to the properties of elliptic curve multiplication, both arrive at the same 32-byte shared secret:

shared_secret = ECDH(client_private, server_public) = ECDH(server_private, client_public) This is the same math behind our ECC key generator and ECDH key exchange tool.

TLS 1.3 uses HKDF (HMAC-based Key Derivation Function, defined in RFC 5869) to derive all session keys from the shared secret. The process involves:

early_secret = HKDF-Extract(salt: 0, key: 0) — initial extraction derived_secret = HKDF-Expand-Label(early_secret, "derived", empty_hash) — bridging to handshake handshake_secret = HKDF-Extract(derived_secret, shared_secret) — core secret client_hs_key = HKDF-Expand-Label(handshake_secret, "c hs traffic", hello_hash) — client handshake key server_hs_key = HKDF-Expand-Label(handshake_secret, "s hs traffic", hello_hash) — server handshake key The HKDF is built on top of HMAC — the same primitive we cover in our HMAC guide. Each expansion step uses HMAC-SHA256 or HMAC-SHA384 depending on the cipher suite.

After the handshake is verified, new keys are derived for actual data encryption:

application_secret = HKDF-Expand-Label(handshake_secret, "c ap traffic" / "s ap traffic", ...) client_app_key = HKDF-Expand-Label(application_secret, "key", ...) client_app_iv = HKDF-Expand-Label(application_secret, "iv", ...) These are the keys that encrypt your HTTP requests and responses.

Phase 4: Encrypted Handshake (Server Authentication) From this point on, all remaining handshake messages are encrypted — a major improvement over TLS 1.2, where the server certificate was sent in the clear.

EncryptedExtensions — non-critical extensions (hidden from eavesdroppers) Certificate — the server's X.509 certificate chain (the same PEM format our PEM certificate parser can decode) CertificateVerify — a digital signature over the entire handshake transcript, proving the server possesses the private key corresponding to the certificate's public key Finished — a MAC (message authentication code) over the entire handshake, ensuring no tampering occurred The client verifies:

The certificate chain up to a trusted root CA The CertificateVerify signature using the certificate's public key The Finished MAC Crypto primitives involved: Digital signatures (RSA-PSS or Ed25519/ECDSA), SHA hashing for the transcript hash, HMAC for the Finished MAC.

Phase 5: Client Authentication (Optional) In most web browsing, only the server is authenticated. But in mutual TLS (mTLS), the client also sends a certificate and CertificateVerify. This is common in API-to-API communication, zero-trust architectures, and enterprise environments.

Phase 6: Application Data The handshake is complete. Both sides now use the negotiated symmetric cipher (AES-256-GCM, AES-128-GCM, or ChaCha20-Poly1305) to encrypt all application data. Each record is independently encrypted with a unique nonce derived from the IV and a sequence number.

Where Each Crypto Primitive Fits Here's the complete picture of how TLS combines every cryptographic primitive:

Phase Primitive TLS 1.3 Usage Our Tool Client Hello Random generation ClientRandom (32 bytes) Random Bytes Key Exchange Elliptic curve DH X25519 or P-256 key agreement ECC Key Gen / ECDH Key Derivation HMAC / HKDF All key schedule operations HMAC Generator Server Auth Digital signature CertificateVerify (RSA-PSS / Ed25519 / ECDSA) Digital Signature Server Auth Hash function Transcript hash (SHA-256 / SHA-384) SHA Hash Server Auth X.509 certificate Server identity proof CSR Generator / PEM Parser Data Encryption AEAD cipher AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 AES Encrypt TLS is not a single algorithm — it is a symphony of every primitive we've discussed across this blog. If you understand AES, RSA, ECC, SHA, and HMAC individually, TLS is where they all come together.

TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3: What Changed Feature TLS 1.2 (2008) TLS 1.3 (2018) Handshake round trips 2-RTT (full) 1-RTT (full), 0-RTT (resumption) Cipher suites 37+ (including RC4, 3DES, CBC) 3 (all AEAD) Key exchange RSA, DH, ECDH, DHE, ECDHE ECDHE only (mandatory forward secrecy) Handshake encryption Server cert sent in clear Entire handshake after ServerHello is encrypted RSA key transport Supported Removed — breaks forward secrecy CBC mode ciphers Supported Removed — vulnerable to padding oracle attacks Compression Supported (vulnerable to CRIME) Removed Renegotiation Supported (complex, risky) Removed Static DH Supported Removed — no forward secrecy Signature algorithms Negotiated implicitly Explicit signature_algorithms extension PSK resumption Session IDs / tickets PSK with (EC)DHE or alone The 1-RTT Handshake (TLS 1.3) Client Server ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── ClientHello (key_share + supported_groups) ──────────────────────────────────────────→ ServerHello (key_share) {EncryptedExtensions} {Certificate} {CertificateVerify} {Finished} ←────────────────────────────────────────── {Client Finished} ──────────────────────────────────────────→ [Application Data] ←──────────────────────→ [Application Data] Messages in {braces} are encrypted. The entire exchange after ServerHello is protected — an eavesdropper cannot see the server's certificate or what algorithms were actually used.

The 0-RTT Resumption If the client has connected to the server before, it can send data in the very first message using a Pre-Shared Key (PSK) from the previous session:

Client Server ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── ClientHello (key_share + PSK_identity + early_data) [Early Application Data] ← sent immediately! ──────────────────────────────────────────→ ServerHello (PSK acceptance) {EncryptedExtensions} ... ←────────────────────────────────────────── Tradeoff: 0-RTT data is not forward secret — if the PSK is compromised, the early data can be decrypted. It is also vulnerable to replay attacks — an attacker can capture and retransmit the 0-RTT message. For this reason, 0-RTT is only safe for idempotent requests (GET, HEAD) and should never be used for state-changing operations like payments or password changes.

Forward Secrecy: Why It Matters Forward secrecy (or perfect forward secrecy, PFS) means that compromising a long-term private key does not compromise past session keys.

In TLS 1.2 with static RSA key exchange, the server's RSA private key was used to decrypt the pre-master secret sent by the client. If an attacker recorded encrypted traffic and later obtained the server's RSA private key, they could decrypt all past sessions.

In TLS 1.3, all key exchange uses ephemeral ECDH. The server generates a fresh ECDH key pair for every single connection. Even if the server's long-term signing key is compromised, past sessions remain secure because the ephemeral ECDH private keys were discarded immediately after use.

Scenario Static RSA (TLS 1.2) Ephemeral ECDH (TLS 1.3) Server private key leaked All past sessions decryptable Past sessions remain secure Recording + later key compromise Traffic exposed Traffic safe Per-session key independence No Yes This is why TLS 1.3 removed static RSA and static DH entirely — they cannot provide forward secrecy by design.

Cipher Suites in Detail TLS 1.3 defines exactly three cipher suites. Each is an AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) algorithm:

TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 Encryption: AES-128 in GCM mode Key size: 128 bits Nonce size: 96 bits (12 bytes) Authentication tag: 128 bits Hash: SHA-256 (for HKDF and transcript) Security level: 128-bit Best for: General-purpose web traffic; hardware-accelerated on most modern CPUs (AES-NI) TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 Encryption: AES-256 in GCM mode Key size: 256 bits Nonce size: 96 bits Authentication tag: 128 bits Hash: SHA-384 Security level: 256-bit Best for: High-security applications; slightly slower than AES-128-GCM without hardware acceleration TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 Encryption: ChaCha20 stream cipher Key size: 256 bits Nonce size: 96 bits Authentication: Poly1305 MAC (128-bit tag) Hash: SHA-256 Security level: 256-bit Best for: Devices without AES hardware acceleration (mobile phones, ARM servers); resistant to cache-timing attacks that affect AES All three provide authenticated encryption — meaning they simultaneously encrypt data for confidentiality and generate an authentication tag for integrity. This eliminates the need for a separate HMAC on the data (unlike TLS 1.2's CBC mode, which required encrypt-then-MAC or MAC-then-encrypt).

For a deep dive into the symmetric algorithms, see our guides on AES-256 encryption and understand how AES compares to ChaCha20 in performance and security characteristics.

Certificate Authentication: The Trust Chain TLS 1.3 servers authenticate using X.509 certificates — the same certificates generated via our CSR generator and parseable by our PEM certificate parser.

End-entity certificate — contains the server's public key and domain name, signed by a CA Intermediate CA certificate(s) — signed by the root CA, used to limit root CA exposure Root CA certificate — pre-installed in the client's trust store (browser or OS) The client verifies:

Each certificate's signature using the issuer's public key Validity dates and domain names Revocation status (via OCSP or CRL) Certificate Transparency (CT) logs for public trust Certificate Types Type Validation Trust Level Use Case DV (Domain Validated) Domain ownership only Basic Blogs, personal sites OV (Organization Validated) Business identity + domain Medium Business websites EV (Extended Validation) Rigorous business verification Highest Banking, e-commerce For more on how certificates are requested and signed, see our guide on Certificate Signing Requests.

Practical TLS Configuration Server-Side Recommendations For nginx:

ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_ciphers ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305; ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off; # Let the client choose ssl_ecdh_curve X25519:secp256r1:secp384r1; ssl_session_timeout 1d; ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:50m; ssl_stapling on; ssl_stapling_verify on; For Apache:

SSLProtocol all -SSLv3 -TLSv1 -TLSv1.1 SSLCipherSuite ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305 SSLHonorCipherOrder off What to Avoid Deprecated / Dangerous Why TLS 1.0 / 1.1 No AEAD, vulnerable to BEAST, POODLE, Lucky13 RSA key exchange No forward secrecy CBC mode ciphers Padding oracle vulnerabilities RC4, 3DES, DES Known cryptographic weaknesses SHA-1 for signatures Collision attacks demonstrated Export-grade ciphers Intentionally weak (FREAK, Logjam) Compression CRIME / BREACH attacks Testing Your Configuration SSL Labs Server Test — comprehensive grade (A+ to F) for your TLS setup testssl.sh — command-line tool that checks for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations cryptcheck.fr — quick grade-based assessment TLS Beyond HTTPS While HTTPS is the most visible use case, TLS also protects:

Protocol Over TLS? Description HTTPS Yes (port 443) Web browsing SMTPS Yes (port 465/587) Email submission IMAPS Yes (port 993) Email retrieval FTPS Yes (port 990) File transfer MQTTS Yes (port 8883) IoT messaging DNS over TLS Yes (port 853) Encrypted DNS resolution DNS over HTTPS Yes (port 443) DNS within HTTPS XMPP Optional Instant messaging IRC Optional (port 6697) Chat Quantum Threats to TLS Current TLS 1.3 relies on two quantum-vulnerable primitives:

ECDH key exchange — Shor's algorithm on a sufficiently large quantum computer could compute the shared secret from the exchanged public keys RSA/ECDSA signatures — Shor's algorithm could forge CertificateVerify signatures Post-quantum TLS is being actively standardized:

ML-KEM (Kyber) for key exchange — replaces or supplements ECDH ML-DSA (Dilithium) or SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) for signatures — replaces RSA/ECDSA Hybrid modes (e.g., X25519 + ML-KEM-768) provide dual security: even if one algorithm is broken, the other still protects the session Major browsers (Chrome, Firefox) have already experimented with hybrid key exchange using X25519 + Kyber (now ML-KEM). See our Post-Quantum Cryptography guide for the full picture.

Troubleshooting Checklist If your TLS connection is failing or showing warnings:

Certificate expired — check notAfter date in the server certificate Wrong hostname — certificate CN/SAN must match the requested domain Incomplete chain — server must send intermediate certificates (not just the leaf) Protocol mismatch — client requires TLS 1.3 but server only supports TLS 1.2 Cipher suite mismatch — no common cipher suite between client and server Revoked certificate — check OCSP stapling or CRL distribution Self-signed certificate — client must explicitly trust the certificate or its CA HSTS preload — if the domain is in the HSTS preload list, HTTP will be rejected Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between TLS and SSL? TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the successor to SSL (Secure Sockets Layer). SSL was the original protocol developed by Netscape in the 1990s. When the IETF standardized it, they renamed it TLS. TLS 1.0 was essentially SSL 3.1. All modern implementations use TLS — SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are deprecated and insecure. When people say "SSL certificate," they actually mean a TLS certificate.

Does TLS use symmetric or asymmetric encryption? Both. TLS uses asymmetric encryption (ECDH + digital signatures) during the handshake to securely exchange keys and authenticate identities. Then it switches to symmetric encryption (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) for the actual data transfer, because symmetric encryption is roughly 100–1000x faster for bulk data. This hybrid design gives you the best of both worlds: the key distribution advantages of asymmetric crypto and the performance of symmetric crypto.

What is forward secrecy and why does TLS 1.3 require it? Forward secrecy means that even if a long-term private key is compromised in the future, past session keys remain secure. TLS 1.3 achieves this by using ephemeral ECDH for every connection — the server generates a fresh key pair each time and discards the private key after the session. This prevents an attacker who records encrypted traffic from decrypting it later, even if they obtain the server's certificate private key.

What is 0-RTT and is it safe? 0-RTT (Zero Round-Trip Time) allows a returning client to send data in the very first message using a pre-shared key from a previous session. It reduces latency but comes with two caveats: (1) 0-RTT data is not forward secret, and (2) it is vulnerable to replay attacks — an attacker can capture and retransmit the 0-RTT message. Use 0-RTT only for idempotent requests like GET.

Which cipher suite should I prefer? For most use cases, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 provides the strongest security. On mobile devices or CPUs without AES hardware acceleration, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 may be faster while still providing 256-bit security. TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 is perfectly adequate for general web traffic and is the most commonly negotiated suite.

Can TLS 1.3 be broken by quantum computers? Not yet — but a large enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could break the ECDH key exchange and RSA/ECDSA signatures that TLS 1.3 relies on. The solution is post-quantum TLS using algorithms like ML-KEM (Kyber) for key exchange and ML-DSA (Dilithium) for signatures. Hybrid modes combining classical and post-quantum algorithms are already being tested in Chrome and Firefox.

Further Reading RFC 8446 — The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3 — The definitive specification RFC 8996 — Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 — Official deprecation of legacy versions RFC 5869 — HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF) — The key derivation mechanism used by TLS 1.3 The Illustrated TLS 1.3 Connection — Byte-by-byte walkthrough of every handshake message SSL Labs — TLS Deployment Best Practices — Mozilla's recommended configurations NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 — Guidelines for TLS Implementations — U.S. government TLS requirements CA/Browser Forum — Baseline Requirements — Certificate issuance standards ACME Protocol (RFC 8555) — Automated Certificate Management (Let's Encrypt) Related Articles AES-256 Encryption — The symmetric cipher that encrypts most TLS 1.3 data traffic Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) — The math behind ECDH key exchange and ECDSA signatures in TLS RSA-2048 Encryption — Still used in some TLS certificate signatures, though being phased out How Digital Signatures Work — The CertificateVerify message that proves server identity HMAC Message Authentication — The building block of HKDF, which derives all TLS session keys Post-Quantum Cryptography — The future of TLS in a quantum computing world

#9704. 3 Personality Traits Associated With Infidelity

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner.

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner.

People who are low on conscientiousness are more likely to cheat on their partner, research finds.

People who are not conscientious are careless, badly organised and find it hard to resist temptation.

People who are more extraverted are also more likely to cheat on their partner, the researchers found.

It is probably because extraverted people have a wider social circle and so more opportunities to cheat.

Also, extraverts are impulsive, sensation-seekers who can easily succumb to their desires.

The conclusions come from a survey of 208 people, who were asked about their relationships and whether they had cheated.

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner, the authors write:

“Early studies reported that by the age of 40, 50% of all married men and more than 25% of all married women have engaged in extramarital sexual behavior.

Three decades later, an estimated 50% of men continued to engage in sexual and/or emotional extramarital relations while 40% of women engaged in similar relationships.”

The results of the study revealed that cheaters tend to be low in conscientiousness, extraverted and open to experience.

Extraverts tend to seek out stimulation, the authors write:

“Extroverts may be inclined to cheat to obtain stimulation and prevent boredom.

Extroversion may also facilitate less investment in the relationship when those with this trait seek out others for stimulation, thereby decreasing commitment and resulting in cheating behaviours.”

The third personality trait associated with infidelity is openness to experience.

Openness to experience is linked to intellect and creativity.

“…cheaters may perceive themselves as having stronger intellect and stronger creativity compared to that of their partners, leading them to seek out partners that may be a better, that is, similar, match.”

The study was published in the journal Current Psychology (Orzeck & Lung, 2005).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9703. Your Website Has Traffic, But Google Analytics Shows Zero Visitors. Here's Why.

You've launched your website. Google Search Console shows impressions and clicks. People are discovering your pages through Google Search. Your website is receiving real traffic.

But when you open Google Analytics 4 (GA4), something strange happens.

Zero visitors. Zero pageviews. Almost no activity.

You check your website source code. The Google Analytics script is there. Your Measurement ID looks correct. There are no obvious JavaScript errors.

This is a frustrating problem because everything can look correct while your analytics system silently fails to collect the events you actually need.

I've explored this problem from a practical development perspective, and there are several important things every developer should understand before trusting their analytics dashboard.

One of the biggest misconceptions about Google Analytics is that adding its tracking script automatically means everything is configured correctly.

The script loads. The Measurement ID exists. The configuration runs.

But there are still several things that can go wrong:

The important lesson: Never assume that analytics works just because the tracking script exists in your HTML.

You need to verify the actual events being sent.

Google Search Console and Google Analytics 4 are not measuring the same activity.

Google Search Console (GSC) tells you how your website performs in Google Search.

Google Analytics 4 (GA4) measures activity on your website when its tracking system successfully collects events.

These numbers don't necessarily indicate that Google is reporting incorrect information.

They indicate that the two systems are observing different stages of the user journey.

Google Search Console can record a search click without your website successfully sending a GA4 event.

For example, a visitor might open your website, but:

This explains why Search Console activity and Analytics activity can differ.

If GSC shows real clicks but GA4 shows nothing, investigate your tracking implementation before assuming your website has no visitors.

Modern websites don't all work like traditional static HTML websites.

Frameworks such as Next.js use different rendering strategies, including:

Some websites also inject scripts through reverse proxies, gateways, or server-side middleware.

These approaches can introduce additional tracking challenges.

For example, imagine a website where the gateway injects Google Analytics directly into the HTML response.

The browser receives the tracking script as part of the rendered HTML.

This approach can work perfectly well, but developers need to understand where and when the script executes.

For SSR applications, inspect the actual HTML delivered to the browser.

Don't rely exclusively on your React components or application source code.

Then search the downloaded HTML for your Measurement ID:

You can also open DevTools and inspect the Network tab to see whether the analytics requests are actually being sent.

This is where things become particularly interesting.

Google Analytics 4 uses an event-based measurement model.

Instead of simply counting page visits, GA4 receives events such as:

A website can load the Google Analytics library successfully but still fail to send the expected events.

This is a basic example of sending a pageview event.

However, the configuration must match the GA4 implementation, and the event must reach the correct measurement destination.

Don't just copy code from an old tutorial and assume it is correct for your setup.

Check the current Google Analytics documentation for the supported event parameters and configuration.

https://developers.google.com/analytics/devguides/collection/ga4

If GA4 reports zero visitors, don't immediately rewrite your entire tracking implementation.

Compare it with the ID used by your website.

Make sure you're checking the correct GA4 property.

Look for requests sent to Google Analytics collection endpoints, particularly:

Check whether the requests are successful.

A successful network response is useful evidence, but it doesn't independently prove that every event has been processed and displayed in your reports.

Also inspect the request payload and confirm:

DebugView is one of the most useful tools for diagnosing event tracking.

Google Analytics → Admin → Data Display → DebugView

Then enable debug mode for your test browser.

Reload your website and interact with it.

If events appear in DebugView, your implementation is sending events that GA4 can receive in debug mode.

If nothing appears, investigate the browser requests, configuration, consent settings, and measurement destination.

Visit your website from another browser or device.

Remember that Realtime and DebugView serve different purposes. DebugView is especially useful for inspecting individual test events.

If you use client-side navigation, move between pages without refreshing the browser.

Check whether each page generates the expected pageview event.

This is especially important for Next.js applications and other single-page application architectures.

Fixing missing analytics events is only half the job.

Another common problem is duplicate tracking.

Imagine you have enabled automatic pageview tracking through GA4 configuration:

Depending on your configuration, both mechanisms may send pageviews for the same navigation.

One actual visit can generate multiple pageview events.

Your dashboard starts reporting inflated numbers.

The solution is to establish one clear owner for pageview tracking.

If automatic tracking handles initial pageviews, don't send another initial pageview manually.

If you implement manual route tracking, configure automatic pageview behavior appropriately and ensure that route changes are tracked exactly once.

For example, a manual configuration might look like:

You can then send pageview events through your own route-tracking implementation.

However, be careful: disabling automatic pageviews also means you must correctly handle the initial pageview and subsequent navigation events yourself.

Before considering your analytics implementation complete, verify these items.

One mistake developers make is treating analytics as a feature that is finished once the integration code is deployed.

In reality, analytics needs its own testing and verification process.

This is why I recommend adding analytics verification to your deployment checklist.

After every major deployment, test the live website.

Verify the actual network requests, inspect the events, and confirm that the expected data reaches the correct property.

Your goal isn't to force every visitor to be tracked. Your goal is to ensure that tracking works correctly when collection is permitted.

Google Analytics problems aren't always caused by missing scripts or incorrect Measurement IDs.

Sometimes the tracking code is installed, the website is working, and Google Search Console is reporting real traffic, but the event implementation is still broken.

Other times, the problem is the opposite: multiple tracking systems are sending the same events and inflating your numbers.

Don't just check whether Google Analytics is installed. Check whether the right events are actually being sent, received, and measured.

For developers working with Next.js, SSR, reverse proxies, or custom analytics integrations, this distinction can save hours of debugging.

Because at the end of the day, having analytics code in your website and having reliable analytics data are two completely different things.

#9702. Preventing Cache Stampedes Caused by Synchronized Redis TTL Expirations: Architecture and Jitter Implementation Patterns

In distributed backend architectures, caching layers (such as Redis or Memcached) are deployed to shield primary databases from high-throughput read operations. However, an architectural oversight in TTL (Time-To-Live) management can transform your caching layer into a single point of catastrophic failure.

Consider a scenario where master data or batched records—say, tens of thousands of catalog items or user configurations—are populated into Redis on a fixed hourly schedule. To keep the cache fresh, every record is assigned an identical TTL: TTL = 3600 (exactly one hour).

In this setup, exactly 3,600 seconds after insertion, tens of thousands of keys expire within the exact same millisecond window. When high-concurrency client traffic lands at that instant:

This phenomenon—widely termed a Cache Stampede, Dogpile Effect, or Thundering Herd—causes connection pool exhaustion, memory saturation, and CPU throttling on the database. In severe production incidents, this cascade triggers timeouts across downstream microservices and ultimately takes down the entire application.

The primary goal in mitigating batch-induced stampedes is straightforward: prevent cached entries from expiring at the identical point in time.

Rather than setting a deterministic, fixed TTL, we introduce bounded pseudo-random noise (jitter) to the expiration interval.

Given a baseline duration $T_{\text{base}}$ and a configurable jitter window $J$, the effective TTL $T_{\text{effective}}$ is computed dynamically:

$$T_{\text{effective}} = \max(1, T_{\text{base}} + \text{UniformRandom}(-J, J))$$

This simple transformation diffuses key evictions across an interval of $[T_{\text{base}} - J, T_{\text{base}} + J]$, smoothing out backend database queries into a continuous, manageable stream rather than an impulse load spike.

Even with jitter in place, unexpected upstream database spikes or temporary networking partitions can cause read latency to surge. If the cache manager continuously bombards a struggling database with read queries upon every miss, it triggers cascading failures.

To address this, the cache layer should integrate an embedded Circuit Breaker pattern. When sequential backend fetch failures exceed a defined error threshold, the circuit transitions to an OPEN state. During this cooldown window, the system immediately returns a lightweight fallback payload (degraded mode) without touching the database, granting the backend time to recover.

The following complete Python implementation demonstrates a resilient cache manager. It incorporates:

💡 For immediate deployment: The complete source code suite (ZIP) for this architecture is available on Gumroad for $0+ (Pay What You Want).

In _calculate_jittered_ttl, a uniform discrete random integer within $[-J, J]$ is applied to the baseline TTL. In high-jitter setups where $J \ge T_{\text{base}}$, an unbounded negative calculation could yield non-positive TTLs, causing Redis to immediately delete the key or trigger runtime errors. The max(1, base_ttl + jitter) safeguard ensures that regardless of the jitter magnitude, every key retains a strictly positive TTL.

A standard cache layer without error boundaries acts as a pass-through when things go wrong: if the database slows down, cache misses increase, which floods the database with even more queries.

By tracking consecutive upstream errors rather than simple cache misses, ResilientCacheManager isolates transient database failures. Once the failure threshold is crossed, the circuit breaker opens for _circuit_cooldown seconds, instantly short-circuiting expensive queries and shedding load until the database recovers.

Encoding and decoding performance in caching layers is critical when handling tens of thousands of requests per second. The implementation leverages orjson (a fast Rust-backed C-extension) when available, while providing a pure-Python fallback to json. This design provides maximum performance in production container environments without breaking developer workstations or lightweight environments where binary dependencies may not be installed.
